props.title: Bob Roberts
props.initialSlug: A folk singer runs for Senate with sinister motives

sections.content: Bob Roberts revolutionized political mockumentaries by skewering right-wing populism through the story of a folk-singing conservative Senate candidate. Tim Robbins' directorial debut masterfully predicted the intersection of celebrity, media manipulation, and political extremism that would come to define modern politics. Like A Face in the Crowd (1957), it shows how entertainment and demagoguery create a dangerous cocktail. The film's brilliant fake folk songs ("Times Are Changin' Back") perfectly parody Bob Dylan while revealing Roberts' insidious messaging.

sections.content: The 1990s saw a wave of politically-charged satires responding to media manipulation and campaign theatrics. Wag the Dog (1997) showed how easily manufactured stories could drive public opinion, while Primary Colors (1998) fictionalized Bill Clinton's first presidential campaign. But Bob Roberts stands out for predicting how conservative movements would appropriate counter-cultural aesthetics - Roberts uses folk music, traditionally associated with progressive causes, to push a reactionary agenda.

The mockumentary format proves particularly effective in Bob Roberts, building on techniques pioneered by This Is Spinal Tap (1984). Through fake news footage, campaign ads, and behind-the-scenes moments, Robbins creates a complete political universe that feels disturbingly real. The film's prescience about conspiracy theories, media echo chambers, and the rise of celebrity politicians makes it even more relevant today than on release. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Political Satire

sections.content: While earlier political films like Dr. Strangelove (1964) used broad satire to tackle serious issues, Bob Roberts helped establish a more documentary-influenced approach that would influence later works like In the Loop (2009) and Death of Stalin (2017). The film's mix of comedy and genuine dread about democratic institutions would become increasingly common in political satires of the 21st century, from Idiocracy (2006) to Vice (2018).
